title: Hard news
hookLine: on hearing of a death, Jews bless "the true judge", a blessing inside grief

lines: A CALL AT AN ODD HOUR.
cards: The phone rings at an odd hour, or a message starts with I'm so sorry. Someone has died. The mind goes blank, or it races.
People reach for words and find the wrong ones: everything happens for a reason, at least they're not suffering, I know how you feel. Silence is hard to bear, so people fill it.
Jewish tradition has words for this moment too, just three of them, said on hearing of a death. Then, just as important, a way of saying nothing more. Today: Dayan HaEmet.

teach.b: Baruch Dayan HaEmet means blessed is the true judge.

teach.h: BLESS OVER THE BAD AS THE GOOD.
teach.b: The Mishnah says that on good news, you bless the one who is good and does good, and on bad news, you bless the true judge.

Then it adds something startling: a person is obligated to bless over the bad just as over the good. That doesn't mean pretending the bad is good. The blessing doesn't say this is fine, and it explains nothing.
It says, in the worst moment: God is still God, and I'm still speaking to God, even through this. Many say the short form, those three words, on hearing of a death.
Close mourners say the full blessing, with God's name, at the funeral, when they tear a piece of their clothing, keriah, an ancient sign of grief.
People often think of Job, who lost everything: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then, the silence.
When the priest Aaron lost two sons, the Torah says: "And Aaron held his peace."
When Job's friends came to comfort him, they sat with him on the ground for seven days without a word, because they saw how great his pain was. Their trouble started when they began to explain.

teach.h: THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.
teach.b: At a shiva house, where mourners sit for seven days, visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first. You arrive with your presence, not a speech. Three words of blessing, then no explanations at all.

how: On hearing of a death, many Jews say Baruch Dayan HaEmet; close mourners say the full blessing when they tear their garment (keriah) at the funeral, and visitors to a shiva house traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first.

o: a prayer asking God to judge a person fairly
blessed is the true judge, said on hearing of a death
a mourner's prayer said every day for a year

games.q: what's inside the hard word — tap the pairs.

s: the blessing says everything happens for a reason
it explains nothing; it says God is still God, even here.
the Mishnah says to bless over the bad as over the good
a person is obligated to bless over bad news just as over good.
Job's friends comforted him best when they were silent
they sat seven days without a word; trouble came when they began to explain.

games.q: you walk into a shiva house. the mourner is sitting low, looking at the floor. you've prepared something to say. what does tradition suggest?
o: say your words right away, to fill the silence.
sit, and wait for the mourner to speak first.
explain why this might be for the best.
games.why: visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first: presence before words, and no explanations.

practice: Let someone you've lost come to mind, or a loss of another kind, or someone else's grief you've witnessed, and don't look for the reason; just let it sit beside you, the way Job's friends sat beside him on the ground.
If you pray, you can say the three words, Dayan HaEmet; if you don't, simply let the silence hold it.

wordCard.voice: Dayan HaEmet. The true judge: the heart of the three words said on hearing of a death, a blessing inside grief that explains nothing.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessed is the true judge. emet, truth, is spelled with the first, middle and last letters of the alphabet.

carryVoice: Your line: even here, a word. Three words, and then presence. I'll see you tomorrow.

sources.q: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 9:2, 9:5 (the true judge; bless over the bad)
Babylonian Talmud, Moed Katan 28b (mourner speaks first)
